lead: The Nyquist plot is the polar plot of G(jω)H(jω) closed over a contour that wraps the right half of the s-plane. Its purpose is to count closed-loop right-half-plane poles without solving the characteristic equation. The count is an encirclement count around −1. Engineers use it to test stability when a parameter, often gain K, varies, and to see how close a design is to instability. It handles open-loop poles on the imaginary axis with small detours. See polar plots for the ω≥0 curve this chapter closes.
prereq: You need: 4.4 polar plots, the characteristic equation and Routh-Hurwitz from Unit 3, and complex mapping of a contour.

blocks.text: The Nyquist contour is a closed path in the s-plane. Start at s=−j∞ on the imaginary axis, go up the jω axis to s=+j∞, then follow a large semicircle of radius R→∞ through the right half-plane back to −j∞. It encloses the entire right half-plane. If G(s)H(s) has a pole on the jω axis, push a small semicircle of radius r→0 into the right half-plane around that pole, so the contour does not pass through the pole.

Mapping every point of this contour through G(s)H(s) gives the Nyquist plot. The open-loop transfer function is G(s)H(s); s=σ+jω is the complex frequency; the critical point is −1+j0. The plot is not just the usual ω≥0 curve: it includes the negative-frequency mirror and the large semicircle image.

blocks.where: N is the number of clockwise encirclements of −1 by the Nyquist plot; P is the number of open-loop poles of G(s)H(s) in the right half-plane; Z is the number of closed-loop poles in the right half-plane. Closed-loop stability needs Z=0, so N=−P. If N is counted counterclockwise, the formula becomes Z=P−N; choose one convention and keep it.

items: Write G(s)H(s) and find all open-loop poles. Count P.
Mark any pole on the jω axis and add the small detour.
Sketch or compute G(jω)H(jω) for ω from 0 to ∞, then mirror for negative ω. Add the image of the large semicircle.
Count clockwise encirclements of −1. Call it N.

blocks.text: Encirclement means the plot makes a full loop around −1, not merely passes near it. A plot that crosses the negative real axis left of −1 and returns on the other side can enclose the point.

sections.h3: Type 0, Type 1, Type 2 plots and gain

blocks.text: The system type is the number of open-loop poles at s=0. A Type 0 system has none. Its Nyquist plot starts at a finite point on the real axis for ω=0 and ends at the origin. A Type 1 system has one pole at s=0. The small detour around the origin sends the plot to a large semicircle at infinity; the ω=0+ branch comes in from infinity along an asymptote. A Type 2 system has two poles at s=0; its small detour produces an even larger sweep at infinity. These infinities are the images of the detour, not values of G(jω) at ω=0.

Increasing gain K multiplies every point of the plot by K. The shape does not change; the plot expands from the origin. For a stable open-loop system (P=0), the closed-loop system is stable while the plot does not enclose −1. The critical gain is the K that makes the plot pass exactly through −1. Below it, N=0 and Z=0. Above it, the plot encloses −1 and Z>0: closed-loop poles move into the right half-plane. For the example below, K=6 is critical; above it two closed-loop poles enter the right half-plane.

Relative stability is the distance from the plot to −1. A plot that passes far to the right of −1 has room for extra gain; a plot that nearly touches −1 is close to instability. Gain margin and phase margin measure this distance, and are covered in 4.6.
Some syllabi call the result the Nyquist stability criterion. The count is exact; the sketch only helps you count.

figure.caption: The curve is the Nyquist plot for G(s)H(s)=6/[s(s+1)(s+2)]. It passes through −1 at ω=√2 rad/s. The branch that runs down to −j∞ comes from ω→0+; the branch that runs up to +j∞ is its negative-frequency mirror. The two tails are joined at infinity by the image of the small detour around s=0, through the positive real axis. Increasing K moves the crossing left and makes the plot enclose −1.

spec.aria: Nyquist plot for K=6 crossing the critical point −1 on the negative real axis, mirrored about the real axis.

examples.question: For G(s)H(s)=K/[s(s+1)(s+2)] with K>0, use the Nyquist criterion to find the range of K for closed-loop stability.
steps: Open-loop poles: s=0, s=−1, s=−2. None lie in the right half-plane, so P=0. The pole at s=0 needs a small detour.
The plot crosses the negative real axis when the imaginary part of the denominator is zero: 2ω−ω³=ω(2−ω²)=0. For ω>0, ω=√2≈1.414 rad/s.
At ω=√2 rad/s, the real part of the denominator is −3(√2)²=−6. So G(j√2)H(j√2)=K/(−6)=−K/6.

Set the crossing equal to the critical point: −K/6=−1 gives K=6. For K<6 the crossing is to the right of −1, so N=0 and Z=N+P=0. For K>6 the crossing is left of −1, N=2 clockwise, and Z=2. K=6 puts the plot exactly through −1, which is marginal.
examples.answer: Closed-loop stability holds for 0<K<6; K=6 is marginal, and K>6 is unstable.
examples.check:
import math
omega = math.sqrt(2)
Kcrit = 6.0
crossing = -Kcrit / 6
print(omega)
print(crossing)
print(Kcrit)

traps: Sign convention: if N is clockwise, use Z=N+P. If N is counterclockwise, use Z=P−N. Mixing the two flips the answer.
P counts open-loop right-half-plane poles of G(s)H(s), not closed-loop poles. Z is the closed-loop count you want.
A pole on the jω axis needs a small detour. Without it, the plot is wrong and the encirclement count can change.
A point exactly at −1 is marginal, not stable. Treat it as the boundary of stability, not as an encirclement.
If you use only the ω≥0 polar plot, add its mirror image for negative frequencies before counting encirclements.

quiz.q: State the Nyquist stability criterion using N as clockwise encirclements of −1.
quiz.a: Z=N+P, where P is the number of open-loop right-half-plane poles and Z is the number of closed-loop right-half-plane poles. Closed-loop stability needs Z=0.

quiz.q: Why does a Type 1 system need a small detour around s=0 in the Nyquist contour?
quiz.a: The contour would otherwise pass through the open-loop pole at the origin. A small semicircle into the right half-plane avoids the pole; its image is a large arc at infinity in the Nyquist plot.

quiz.q: For G(s)H(s)=K/[s(s+1)(s+2)] with P=0 and K=10, find N and Z.
quiz.a: The negative-real crossing is at −K/6=−10/6≈−1.667, left of −1. The plot makes two clockwise encirclements, so N=2. Then Z=N+P=2. The closed-loop system has two right-half-plane poles and is unstable.

quiz.q: A system has P=2 open-loop right-half-plane poles. Its Nyquist plot encircles −1 twice counterclockwise. Using N as clockwise encirclements, find Z.
quiz.a: Two counterclockwise encirclements mean N=−2. Then Z=N+P=−2+2=0. The closed-loop system is stable.

quiz.q: What is the critical point in the Nyquist plot?
quiz.a: The critical point is −1+j0 on the complex plane.

quiz.q: What happens to the Nyquist plot when gain K is increased?
quiz.a: Every point is multiplied by K, so the plot scales outward from the origin. The shape stays the same, but crossings move and the number of encirclements of −1 can change.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Nyquist counting appears in loop-shaping and robust control, where disk margins replace a single critical point to allow gain and phase variation at once. MIMO versions use the determinant of I+G(jω)H(jω) and count encirclements of the origin. Search terms: Nyquist array, disk margin, structured singular value, and small-gain theorem.
